analysis.one_liner: Requires new cars to display a label showing where they were built and what share of parts came from America.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee, which held one hearing in September 1992, and died when the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal auto safety law to require every new car sold in the United States to carry a prominent label stating where the vehicle was produced and the percentage of its parts, by value, made in the United States [S2] [S3]. Enforcement would have run through the existing motor vehicle safety enforcement system, and the Department of Transportation would have had to write the rules within months of enactment [S3]. The goal, per its Buy American framing, was to let car shoppers compare domestic content before buying [S1]. It was introduced by Rep. Curt Weldon with 14 cosponsors from both parties, but the House Energy and Commerce Committee never voted on it [S4] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Car buyers who want to know whether a vehicle and its parts were made in America before they pay; American auto parts makers and assembly plants, whose share of a vehicle's value would be spelled out on every window sticker [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car shoppers and domestic parts makers

how_it_helps.text: Every new car would have to display a prominent label showing the location where it was produced and the percentage of its total value that came from US-made parts, so buyers could compare domestic content across models [S2] [S3].
Enforcement would piggyback on the existing motor vehicle safety enforcement machinery, so violations could be pursued without creating a new agency [S3].

The bill forced quick regulatory action: the Secretary would have had to propose rules within 90 days of enactment, and if final rules were not issued 90 days later, the proposed rules would automatically take effect as final [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers and importers, who would bear the cost of producing and affixing content labels; foreign-brand importers and vehicles with low US content would face the most revealing disclosures, since the label would show shoppers exactly how little of their purchase was made domestically [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: A parts-value percentage is an imperfect signal: it measures where parts were made but not where assembly labor occurred, so a car could earn a high 'US content' number while the jobs that mattered were elsewhere, potentially misleading the shoppers the label was meant to inform [S3].
Manufacturers and importers would bear labeling and compliance costs and would face enforcement penalties for mislabeled vehicles under the safety-law enforcement provisions [S3].

The label has a protectionist edge: its stated subject areas include Buy American and import restrictions, and steering buyers toward high-domestic-content vehicles is meant to help domestic producers, not necessarily to get shoppers a better or cheaper car [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The information benefit to shoppers is real but modest — a single percentage on a sticker, not a full picture of where a car's value and jobs come from — and the compliance cost to automakers is small. The bill was a low-cost transparency measure with a Buy American purpose; its main weakness was that the label could oversimplify domestic content rather than mislead maliciously.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to a subcommittee that held one hearing, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Curt Weldon introduced the bill on February 14, 1992, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
On February 28, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness [S5].
The subcommittee held hearings on September 10, 1992, but no markup or vote ever followed, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].
The bill drew 14 cosponsors from both parties — 10 Democrats and 4 Republicans — but that support was never tested on the floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and importers are better off: no vehicle ever had to disclose where it was built or what share of its parts was American, and domestic parts makers gained nothing from the disclosure they would have benefited from.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers, who never had to label content

for.name: Rep. Curt Weldon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to a subcommittee hearing

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 102nd Congress by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; it sat at subcommittee after one hearing and expired with the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The 14 cosponsors split 10 Democrats to 4 Republicans, so sponsorship was bipartisan; no recorded floor opposition exists because the bill never got that far.

industries.note: The bill would have forced every manufacturer to disclose where a car was built and what share of its parts value was American — a small cost, but a disclosure many sellers would rather avoid because low-domestic-content vehicles would look worse on the sticker. High-domestic-content producers would have gained a marketing edge.

industries.industry: US auto parts suppliers and domestic assembly plants
industries.note: A required US-parts percentage would highlight domestic content, giving American parts makers and assembly plants a visible selling point. Their gain ran alongside the buyer's interest in knowing what they were buying.
Dealers would display and sell vehicles carrying the new labels; the disclosure itself is aimed at manufacturers and importers, and an informed buyer is the point of sale pitch either way.
